title: Engineered Enzyme Reverses a Chemical Hallmark of Aging by Up to 70 Percent in Human Tissue
excerpt: A Nature Communications study describes CMLase, an enzyme that strips away decades of protein damage once thought to be permanent — bringing a 75-year-old's tissue markers closer to those of a 31-year-old.
body:
The Damage That Was Supposed to Be Permanent

Since the 1980s, scientists have treated a particular type of age-related protein damage as irreversible. The damage, known as Nε-carboxymethyl-lysine (CML), is a type of advanced glycation end product — or AGE — that forms when sugars react with proteins in a process similar to the Maillard reaction that browns bread in a toaster.

"Instead of cooking at 400 degrees for 30 minutes, we are cooking at 98 degrees for 50-70 years, and we build up some of the same products as food," Aaron Cravens, CEO of Revel Pharmaceuticals and corresponding author of the study, told The Scientist. "And the body has no way to get rid of them."

These chemical modifications accumulate in long-lived structural proteins — collagen, elastin, and eye lens proteins — contributing to tissue stiffening, chronic inflammation, and accelerated biological aging. A new study published in Nature Communications now demonstrates that this damage can, in fact, be reversed under laboratory conditions.

500 Million Variants to Find the Right Enzyme

The research team, comprising scientists from Revel Pharmaceuticals, Calico (Alphabet's life-sciences subsidiary), and the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, used directed evolution to engineer an enzyme called CMLase from a bacterial glycine oxidase scaffold. The process involved screening more than 500 million enzyme variants to find one capable of precisely targeting and removing CML modifications.

"This class of damage has been seen as a fixed part of aging since the 1980s. What we've shown is that CML damage in human tissue can, in fact, be reversed under laboratory conditions."

— Aaron Cravens, CEO, Revel Pharmaceuticals

Tested on human tissue from donors ranging in age from 20 to 75 years old, CMLase reduced CML levels by more than 70 percent in a 75-year-old donor's arterial tissue and by more than 55 percent in aged donor skin. The treated skin samples showed CML levels below those typically seen in a 31-year-old. Crucially, the enzyme repaired the majority of damage sites across various model proteins while leaving the underlying protein structures intact.

From Lab Bench to Potential Therapy

The Scientist compared the enzyme's mechanism to a "lawnmower" that methodically clears molecular debris. CMLase works by oxidising the CML modification, effectively snipping off the harmful chemical tag that sugar molecules had attached to the protein over decades. The process restores the protein to something closer to its original, undamaged state.

Revel Pharmaceuticals, a San Francisco-based biotech company supported by NIH Small Business Innovation Research grants, is developing a platform of engineered enzymes aimed at reversing accumulated oxidative and glycation damage in aging tissues. The company's broader pipeline also targets crystal accumulation and other forms of structural damage.

What's Next

Cravens acknowledged that "more work is needed," but said the results "alter the starting assumption for how we think about this fundamental aspect of the aging process." The researchers are particularly interested in developing interventions for patient populations that accumulate AGEs at a faster rate, including people with type 2 diabetes.
